q: A student is reviewing the doubling rule, in which stress placement decides whether the final consonant doubles. Which word is spelled correctly?
o: occurence
referrence
openning
referred
w: Re-FER is stressed on the last syllable, so the r doubles before -ed: "referred". Doubling depends on where the stress falls in the new word.

n.0: Oc-CUR is stressed on the last syllable, so the r doubles: "occurrence".
n.1: In REF-er-ence the stress moves to the first syllable, so the r does not double: "reference".
n.2: O-pen is stressed on the first syllable, so the n does not double: "opening".

q: A hospital volunteer is writing an announcement about a parade route. Which of the following words, all ending in a "seed" sound, is spelled correctly?
o: superceed
preceed
proceed
excede
w: Only three common words end in -ceed: exceed, proceed and succeed. Only supersede ends in -sede. All others end in -cede.

n.0: Supersede is the one common word ending in -sede; "superceed" wrongly gives it the -ceed ending.
n.1: Precede takes the regular -cede ending; -ceed is reserved for exceed, proceed and succeed.
n.3: Exceed is one of the three -ceed words, so "excede" is wrong.

q: A student writing a lab report adds prefixes to base words. Which word correctly keeps every letter of both the prefix and the root?
o: disatisfied
imature
unnecessary
mispell
w: Adding a prefix does not change the spelling of the root: un + necessary = "unnecessary", with both n's kept.

n.0: Dis + satisfied keeps both s's: "dissatisfied".
n.1: Im + mature keeps both m's: "immature".
n.3: Mis + spell keeps both s's: "misspell".

q: An editor is checking adverbs formed by adding -ly in a discharge leaflet for patients. Which adverb is spelled correctly?
o: finaly
gentlely
carefuly
publicly
w: "Publicly" is formed by adding -ly straight to public; it is the standard exception to the -ically pattern.

n.0: Final + ly keeps both l's: "finally".
n.1: Adjectives ending in -le replace the e with y: gentle becomes "gently".
n.2: Careful + ly keeps both l's: "carefully".

q: Read the sentence from a hospital newsletter: "The physician noted that the patient's hemorrage had stopped before the anesthesia wore off." Which word in the sentence is misspelled?
o: physician
anesthesia
patient's
hemorrage
w: The correct spelling is "hemorrhage", with r-r-h; the rh comes from the Greek word part -rrhage (bursting forth).

n.0: "Physician" is spelled correctly.
n.1: "Anesthesia" is the correct US spelling (UK: anaesthesia).
n.2: "Patient's" is the correct singular possessive of patient.

q: A nursing applicant is studying a list of commonly misspelled words before the TEAS. Which words are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
o: embarass
occurrence
seperate
definately
privilege
accommodate
w: Accommodate (double c, double m), occurrence (double c, double r) and privilege (i-l-e-g-e) are correct.

n.0: The correct spelling is "embarrass", with double r and double s.
n.2: The correct spelling is "separate", with a after the p.
n.3: The correct spelling is "definitely", from the root finite.

q: A charge nurse is proofreading a sentence for a unit memo. Which version of the sentence is spelled correctly?
o: She was carrying the foreign samples to the lab.
She was carriing the foreign samples to the lab.
She was carrying the foriegn samples to the lab.
She was carriing the foriegn samples to the lab.
w: Two rules apply. Before -ing, a final y is kept (carry + ing = carrying). "Foreign" is an exception to i before e and is spelled e-i.

n.1: "Carriing" wrongly changes y to i before -ing; the y is kept: "carrying".
n.2: "Foreign" is an exception spelled e-i, not i-e.
n.3: Both words are wrong: the y must stay before -ing, and "foreign" is spelled e-i.

q: A US health department is editing a brochure for American readers. Which sentence follows standard American spelling throughout?
o: The center will analyze each patient's behaviour.
The center will analyze each patient's behavior.
The center will analyse each patient's behavior.
The centre will analyze each patient's behavior.
w: American English uses -er (center), -yze (analyze) and -or (behavior). Each other version slips in one British spelling.

n.0: "Behaviour" is the British spelling; American English drops the u: "behavior".
n.2: "Analyse" is the British spelling; American English uses "analyze".
n.3: "Centre" is the British spelling; American English uses "center".

q: A nurse is writing an incident note about several patients who share a room on a pediatric unit. Which sentence uses plural and possessive forms correctly?
o: The patients' in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the childrens' toys.
The patient's in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
w: "Patients" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe. "Children" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "children's".

n.0: The patients do not own anything here, so "patients'" (plural possessive) is wrong; the plain plural is needed.
n.2: "Children" already is plural; an irregular plural not ending in s takes 's, so "childrens'" is wrong.
n.3: "Patient's" uses an apostrophe to make a plain plural; plurals that show no ownership take no apostrophe.

q: A hospital kitchen supervisor is writing a short inventory note. Which sentence uses the correct plural form of every noun?
o: The chefs stored the knives on the shelfs.
The chefs stored the knifes on the shelves.
The cheves stored the knives on the shelves.
The chefs stored the knives on the shelves.
w: Many nouns ending in f or fe change to -ves (knife to knives, shelf to shelves), but some simply add s, including chef (chefs).

n.0: Shelf changes f to ves: "shelves".
n.1: Knife changes fe to ves: "knives".
n.2: Chef is an exception to the f-to-ves rule; its plural is "chefs".

q: A physician's note must use standard plural forms. Which sentence uses the correct plural of every noun?
o: Both diagnosis were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnoses were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnosises were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnoses were confirmed after the two analysises.
w: Greek-origin nouns ending in -is form the plural by replacing -is with -es: diagnosis becomes "diagnoses" and analysis becomes "analyses" (like crisis, crises).

n.0: "Diagnosis" is the singular form, but "both" and "were" require the plural "diagnoses".
n.2: The -is ending is replaced, not kept: the plural of diagnosis is "diagnoses", not "diagnosises".
n.3: The -is ending is replaced, not kept: the plural of analysis is "analyses", not "analysises".

q: A clinic's front-desk sign is being revised. Which sentence uses possessive pronouns correctly?
o: The clinic updated it's hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its' hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is your's.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is yours.
w: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose) never take an apostrophe.

n.0: "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; the possessive is "its".
n.1: "Its'" is not a word; the possessive pronoun is "its".
n.2: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun and takes no apostrophe.

q: A newspaper is writing about a local nurse honored for bravery. Which sentence uses the correct plural form of each noun?
o: The article included photos of the local heroes.
The article included photos of the local heros.
The article included photoes of the local heroes.
The article included photoes of the local heros.
w: Two rules apply. Many nouns ending in consonant + o add -es (hero to heroes), but some, including photo, simply add s (photos).

n.1: Hero is a consonant + o noun that adds -es: "heroes".
n.2: Photo is an exception that adds only s: "photos".
n.3: Both are wrong: photo adds s, and hero adds -es.

q: Maria and Lee own one clinic together. Which sentence correctly shows their shared ownership of the clinic?
o: Maria and Lees' clinic opens at eight.
Maria's and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Marias and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Maria and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
w: For joint ownership, only the last name takes the possessive: "Maria and Lee's clinic". Separate possessives (Maria's and Lee's) signal separate ownership.

n.0: Lee is one person, so the singular possessive is "Lee's", not "Lees'".
n.1: Making both names possessive signals individual ownership, which does not fit one shared clinic.
n.2: "Marias" is a plural with no apostrophe; Maria is one person and needs no s here.

q: A staff newsletter describes a nurse's family. Which sentence uses the correct plural of the compound noun?
o: Both of her sisters-in-law work as nurses.
Both of her sister-in-laws work as nurses.
Both of her sister's-in-law work as nurses.
Both of her sisters-in-laws work as nurses.
w: In a hyphenated compound noun, the main word takes the plural: sister becomes sisters, giving "sisters-in-law".

n.1: The s goes on the main word (sister), not the end of the compound.
n.2: An apostrophe shows possession, not plurality; nothing is owned here.
n.3: The compound is pluralized once, on the main word; adding a second s is wrong.

q: Jada has one sister-in-law, who owns a car. Which sentence correctly shows that the car belongs to that one sister-in-law?
o: My sisters-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister's-in-law car is in the shop.
My sister-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister-in-laws car is in the shop.
w: A compound noun forms its possessive on the last word: "sister-in-law's". The singular form is used because there is one owner.

n.0: "Sisters-in-law's" is the plural possessive, but Jada has only one sister-in-law.
n.1: The possessive ending goes on the last word of the compound, not the first.
n.3: "Sister-in-laws" has no apostrophe, so it is not a possessive.

q: A human resources assistant is writing a bonus notice for staff. Which sentence uses possessive forms of time expressions correctly?
o: The bonus equals one week's pay for two weeks' work.
The bonus equals one weeks' pay for two weeks' work.
The bonus equals one week's pay for two week's work.
The bonus equals one weeks pay for two weeks' work.
w: Two steps: one week is singular, so add 's (one week's pay); two weeks is a plural ending in s, so add only an apostrophe (two weeks' work).

n.1: "One week" is singular, so its possessive is "week's", not "weeks'".
n.2: "Two weeks" is plural, so the apostrophe goes after the s: "weeks'".
n.3: "One weeks pay" uses a plural with "one" and leaves out the apostrophe.

q: A hospital historian is writing about staff hired decades ago. Which sentence uses plurals and apostrophes correctly?
o: Several RNs' on the unit were hired in the 1990s.
Several RNs on the unit were hired in the 1990s'.
Several RNs on the unit were hired in the 1990s.
Several RN's on the unit were hired in the 1990s.
w: Plurals of abbreviations and numbers add s with no apostrophe: RNs, 1990s. Nothing in the sentence is possessive.

n.0: "RNs'" is a plural possessive, but the RNs do not own anything here.
n.1: A decade written in numerals takes s with no apostrophe: "1990s".
n.3: An apostrophe is not used to form the plural of an abbreviation such as RN.

q: A student is checking a list of plural nouns for a biology report. Which plurals are formed correctly? Select all that apply.
o: beliefs
attorneys
passerbys
crises
wolfs
stimuluses
w: Crisis becomes crises (-is to -es); attorney adds s because it ends in vowel + y; belief is an f noun that simply adds s.

n.2: In a compound noun the main word is pluralized: "passersby".
n.5: Stimulus is a Latin noun whose plural is "stimuli".

q: Read the sentence from a facilities report: "The mens' locker room and the women's lounge were repainted despite the residents' objections." Which word contains an error?
o: mens'
objections
residents'
women's
w: "Men" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "men's".

n.1: "Objections" is a plain plural that owns nothing, so no apostrophe is needed.
n.2: "Residents'" is correct: a regular plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe.
n.3: "Women's" is correct: an irregular plural not ending in s adds 's.

q: A volunteer coordinator is writing a note about visitors in the hospital lobby. Which sentence uses "their," "there," and "they're" correctly?
o: Their leaving their coats over there by the door.
They're leaving there coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over their by the door.
They're leaving their coats over there by the door.
w: "They're" is the contraction of "they are", "their" shows possession (their coats), and "there" names a place (over there).

n.0: The sentence needs "they are leaving", so the contraction "they're" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.1: The coats belong to them, so the possessive "their" is required, not the place word "there".
n.2: "Over ___" names a place, so "there" is required, not the possessive "their".

q: A nurse is documenting how long a procedure took. Which sentence uses "than" and "then" correctly?
o: The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
w: "Than" makes a comparison (longer than expected); "then" shows time or sequence (and then left).

n.0: "And ___ left" shows sequence, so it needs "then".
n.1: Both are reversed: the comparison needs "than" and the sequence needs "then".
n.2: "Longer ___ expected" is a comparison, so it needs "than".

q: A unit manager is writing a staffing note at the end of a long shift. Which sentence uses "to," "too," and "two" correctly?
o: The two aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The too aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were too tired too finish the charts.
The two aides were to tired to finish the charts.
w: "Two" is the number, "too" means excessively (too tired), and "to" begins the infinitive (to finish).

n.1: The number of aides requires "two".
n.2: An infinitive is formed with "to": "to finish".
n.3: "___ tired" means excessively tired, which requires "too".

q: A receptionist is asking about a missing medical record. Which sentence uses "who's" and "whose" correctly?
o: Who's the patient who's chart is missing?
Whose the patient who's chart is missing?
Whose the patient whose chart is missing?
Who's the patient whose chart is missing?
w: "Who's" is the contraction of "who is" (Who is the patient?); "whose" shows possession (whose chart).

n.0: The chart belongs to the patient, so the possessive "whose" is needed, not "who is".
n.1: Both are reversed: the opening needs "who's" and the possessive needs "whose".
n.2: The sentence opens with "Who is the patient", so it needs the contraction "who's".

q: A patient education sheet describes a medication's results. Which sentence uses "affect" and "effect" correctly?
o: The new medication did not affect her sleep, but it had an affect on her appetite.
The new medication did not effect her sleep, but it had an effect on her appetite.
The new medication did not effect her sleep, but it had an affect on her appetite.
The new medication did not affect her sleep, but it had an effect on her appetite.
w: "Affect" is usually a verb meaning "to influence" (did not affect her sleep); "effect" is usually a noun meaning "result" (an effect on her appetite).

n.0: After the article "an", the noun meaning "result" is needed: "effect".
n.1: "Did not ___ her sleep" needs the verb meaning "influence", which is "affect"; "effect" as a verb means "bring about".
n.2: Both are reversed: the verb should be "affect" and the noun should be "effect".

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The school's ____ explained that honesty is a basic ____ of the honor code."
o: principal; principal
principal; principle
principle; principle
principle; principal
w: "Principal" names the head of a school (or means "main"); "principle" is a rule or belief, as in a principle of the honor code.

n.0: A basic rule of a code is a "principle", not a "principal".
n.2: The head of a school is the "principal", not a "principle".
n.3: Both words are reversed: the school's head is the principal, and a rule is a principle.

q: A physical therapist is writing a home exercise plan. Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The new exercise bike is ____, so it will ____ the walking program."
o: stationery; compliment
stationery; complement
stationary; compliment
stationary; complement
w: "Stationary" means not moving; "complement" means to complete or go well with. A bike that stays in place goes well with a walking program.

n.0: Both are wrong: the bike is stationary (not moving), and it complements (goes well with) the program.
n.1: "Stationery" is writing paper; a bike that does not move is "stationary".
n.2: "Compliment" means to praise; going well with something is "complement".

q: A charge nurse is writing a reminder about patient safety bands. Which sentence uses commonly confused words correctly?
o: All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
w: "Except" means excluding (all except Mr. Ito); "lose" means to misplace (not to lose their wristbands). "Loose" means not tight.

n.0: "Loose" is an adjective meaning not tight; misplacing something is "lose".
n.1: Both are wrong: excluding someone is "except", and misplacing something is "lose".
n.2: "Accept" means to receive; excluding someone requires "except".

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the instruction? "The respiratory therapist will ____ you to take a deep ____ before you exhale slowly."
o: advise; breathe
advice; breathe
advice; breath
advise; breath
w: "Advise" is the verb (will advise you); "breath" is the noun (a deep breath). "Advice" and "breathe" are the noun and verb forms of the other pair.

n.0: After "a deep" a noun is needed: "breath". "Breathe" is a verb.
n.1: Both are reversed: the verb is "advise" and the noun is "breath".
n.2: After "will" a verb is needed: "advise". "Advice" is a noun.

q: Read the sentence from a hospital memo: "The council decided that the new policy would ensure that personnel were not allowed to leave there stations early." Which word is used incorrectly?
o: personnel
ensure
there
council
w: The stations belong to the personnel, so the possessive "their" is required: "leave their stations".

n.0: "Personnel" (staff) is correct; "personal" means private.
n.1: "Ensure" (make certain) is correct; "insure" means to buy insurance.
n.3: "Council" (a group that makes decisions) is correct; "counsel" means advice.

q: A tutor gives a student six sentences to check for commonly confused words. In which sentences is every word used correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The storm is imminent, so stay indoors.
Her new shoes are to tight to wear.
The elicit drugs were seized at the border.
He gave me some good advise yesterday.
She is conscious of the risks involved.
Please cite your sources in the report.
w: "Imminent" means about to happen, "conscious" means aware, and "cite" means to quote or name a source.

n.1: "Excessively tight" requires "too": "too tight to wear".
n.2: Illegal drugs are "illicit"; "elicit" means to draw out.
n.3: After "some good" a noun is needed: "advice". "Advise" is a verb.

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "By the time the team was ____ to begin, the patient had ____ been discharged."
o: all ready; already
all ready; all ready
already; all ready
already; already
w: "All ready" means completely prepared (the team was all ready to begin); "already" means by this time (had already been discharged).

n.1: "Had all ready been discharged" needs the time word "already".
n.2: Both are reversed: being prepared is "all ready", and "by this time" is "already".
n.3: Being completely prepared is "all ready"; "was already to begin" does not make sense.

q: A nursing student is editing a shift report that joins two complete thoughts with a coordinating conjunction. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The nurse checked the patient's chart, and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse, checked the patient's chart and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
w: When a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction: "chart, and the doctor".

n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "and" is needed.
n.2: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.
n.3: A comma must not separate a subject (The nurse) from its verb (checked), and the comma before "and" is missing.

q: An aide's charting note has one subject doing two actions. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The aide measured the patient's, blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide measured the patient's blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide, measured the patient's blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide measured the patient's blood pressure, and recorded it in the chart.
w: This is one subject (The aide) with a compound predicate (measured ... and recorded). With no second subject, there is no second independent clause, so no comma goes before "and".

n.0: A comma must not split a possessive from the noun it modifies.
n.2: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb.
n.3: A comma before "and" is used when it joins two independent clauses; here "recorded it" has no subject of its own.

q: A lab supervisor is writing a note that begins with an introductory dependent clause. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon the samples were stored until Monday.
Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples, were stored until Monday.
Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples were stored until Monday.
Because, the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples were stored until Monday.
w: A long introductory dependent clause (Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon) is followed by a comma before the main clause.

n.0: The comma after the long introductory dependent clause is missing, so the reader runs "afternoon the samples" together.
n.1: A comma must not separate the subject (the samples) from its verb (were stored).
n.3: No comma follows the subordinating conjunction "Because".

q: A hospital bulletin introduces the doctor on call. Which sentence punctuates the nonessential appositive correctly?
o: Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight, will review the scans.
Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight will review the scans.
Dr. Patel the surgeon on call tonight, will review the scans.
Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight, will review, the scans.
w: A nonessential appositive that renames a proper noun is set off by a pair of commas, one before it and one after it.

n.1: The closing comma after "tonight" is missing; a nonessential element needs commas on both sides.
n.2: The opening comma after "Dr. Patel" is missing.
n.3: A comma must not separate the verb (will review) from its object (the scans).

q: A unit has twelve patients, and only one of them fell yesterday. Which sentence correctly identifies that particular patient?
o: The patient who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
w: Two steps: with twelve patients, "who fell yesterday" is essential (restrictive) because it identifies which patient. Essential clauses take no commas.

n.1: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb (needs).
n.2: A single comma after "patient" opens an aside that is never closed.
n.3: Commas would mark the clause as nonessential, as if there were only one patient; here it is needed to identify the patient.

q: A community health newsletter describes a local clinic. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
w: A proper noun is already identified, so the clause "which opened in 2020" is nonessential and needs a pair of commas.

n.1: The closing comma after "2020" is missing.
n.2: The opening comma after "Riverside Clinic" is missing.
n.3: A nonessential clause after a proper noun must be set off with commas.

q: A nurse is writing a reflective journal entry. Which sentence punctuates the adjectives correctly?
o: It was a long, tiring shift in the busy, emergency room.
It was a long, tiring, shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
w: "Long" and "tiring" are coordinate adjectives (they could be joined by "and"), so a comma separates them. "Emergency room" is a compound noun, so "busy" takes no comma.

n.0: "Emergency" is part of the noun "emergency room", so no comma follows "busy".
n.1: No comma goes between the last adjective and the noun it modifies.
n.2: Coordinate adjectives that each describe the noun separately are separated by a comma: "long, tiring".

q: A press release announces a new hospital wing. Which sentence uses commas correctly with the date and the place?
o: On July 4, 2026 the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
On July, 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas opened a new wing.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
w: Two rules apply. In a full date, commas follow the day and the year when the sentence continues. In a city-state pair, commas follow the city and the state.

n.0: The comma after the year "2026" is missing.
n.1: No comma goes between the month and the day.
n.2: The comma after the state "Texas" is missing.

q: A nurse is confirming paperwork with a patient. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Ms. Chen, you finished, the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form didn't you?
w: A name in direct address is set off by a comma, and a tag question (didn't you?) is also set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the verb (finished) from its object, and the comma before the tag question is missing.
n.1: The comma after the name in direct address is missing.
n.3: The comma before the tag question "didn't you" is missing.

q: A medical secretary is proofreading a memo that uses the word "however" in several positions. Which sentence contains a comma error?
o: The results were not available, however until Tuesday.
However, the results were not available until Tuesday.
The results, however, were not available until Tuesday.
The results were not available until Tuesday, however.
w: "However" used as an interrupter in the middle of a clause must be set off by commas on both sides: "available, however, until Tuesday". One comma is missing.

n.1: Correct: an introductory "However" is followed by a comma.
n.2: Correct: the interrupter is enclosed by a pair of commas.
n.3: Correct: a closing "however" is preceded by a comma.

q: A writing tutor gives a student six sentences from patient handouts. Which sentences are punctuated correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The new nurse on the night shift, works weekends.
I stayed late, but, the charts were still unfinished.
The new nurse on the night shift works weekends.
She needs rest, not more medication.
The forms, that you signed, are in the file.
Mr. Ruiz, your lab results are ready.
w: A long subject takes no comma before its verb; a contrasting element (not more medication) is set off by a comma; a name in direct address (Mr. Ruiz) is set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject (The new nurse on the night shift) from its verb.
n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "but" is needed.
n.4: A "that" clause is essential (restrictive), so it takes no commas.

q: Read the paragraph. (1) When flu season began, the clinic extended its hours. (2) Patients could visit on weekday evenings or on Saturday mornings. (3) The clinic hired two nurses and the staff shared the extra shifts. (4) By March, waiting times had dropped. Which sentence needs a comma added?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 3 joins two independent clauses (The clinic hired two nurses / the staff shared the extra shifts) with "and", so a comma is needed before "and". Without it, a reader first takes "two nurses and the staff" as one object.

n.0: Sentence 1 already has the comma after its introductory clause.
n.1: Sentence 2 has one clause; "or" joins two phrases, so no comma is needed.
n.3: Sentence 4 already has its comma after the introductory phrase.

q: A lab technician is writing an update that joins two closely related complete thoughts. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The lab closed early the samples will be tested tomorrow.
Because the lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
w: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no punctuation between them form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.1: "Because the lab closed early" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses, so a comma belongs here.
n.3: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma creates a comma splice.

q: A nurse is charting a change in a patient's plan, using "however" to link two independent clauses. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The patient felt better, however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better; however the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better; however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better however, the doctor ordered one more test.
w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

n.0: Commas on both sides of "however" leave two independent clauses joined by commas, a comma splice.
n.1: The comma after "however" is missing.
n.3: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.

q: An exam-day reminder lists what test takers must bring. Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
o: Bring three items to the exam; your ID, your login, and a pen.
The items to bring are: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring three items to the exam: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring to the exam: your ID, your login, and a pen.
w: A colon introduces a list only after a complete independent clause: "Bring three items to the exam" can stand alone.

n.0: A semicolon does not introduce a list; it joins independent clauses or separates complex series items.
n.1: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "are".
n.3: "Bring to the exam" is incomplete (the verb has no object), so it cannot introduce a list with a colon.

q: A travel nurse lists the cities on her contract schedule. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The tour stops in Boise; Idaho, Reno; Nevada, and Provo; Utah.
The tour stops in: Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour stops in Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour stops in Boise, Idaho, Reno, Nevada, and Provo, Utah.
w: When series items already contain commas (city, state), semicolons separate the items so each pair stays together.

n.0: The semicolons are placed inside each pair instead of between the pairs.
n.1: A colon must not follow a preposition such as "in".
n.3: With commas only, the reader cannot tell where one city-state pair ends and the next begins.

q: Read the sentence from a discharge checklist: "The discharge packet includes: a medication list, a follow-up card, and a diet sheet." Which revision corrects the punctuation error?
o: Move the colon to follow "packet"
Replace the colon with a comma
Delete the colon after "includes"
Replace the colon with a semicolon
w: A colon must not separate a verb (includes) from its objects. Deleting it lets the list follow the verb directly.

n.0: A colon after "packet" would split the subject from its verb, which is also an error.
n.1: A comma must not separate a verb from its objects.
n.3: A semicolon cannot introduce a list or separate a verb from its objects.

q: A wellness coordinator is writing a poster about rest. Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
o: One factor: mattered most to the team, getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team: getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team; getting enough sleep.
The factor that mattered most was: getting enough sleep.
w: A colon after a complete independent clause can introduce an explanation or example: "getting enough sleep" explains the factor.

n.0: A colon must not separate a subject (One factor) from its verb (mattered).
n.2: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "getting enough sleep" is a phrase.
n.3: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "was".

q: A writer wants to set off an interrupting phrase that already contains commas and to give it more emphasis than parentheses would. Which punctuation should enclose the phrase?
o: A pair of colons
A pair of dashes
A pair of semicolons
A pair of brackets
w: A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas or parentheses but gives more emphasis, and it can enclose an element that has its own internal commas.

n.0: A colon introduces a list, explanation or quotation after an independent clause; colons are not used in pairs.
n.2: Semicolons join independent clauses or separate complex series items; they do not enclose interrupters.
n.3: Brackets mark the writer's own insertions inside a quotation.

q: A patient letter ends by pointing readers to an enclosed report. Which sentence uses parentheses correctly?
o: The results were normal (see the attached report.)
The results were normal. (see the attached report)
The results were normal (see the attached report).
The results were normal, (see the attached report).
w: When a parenthetical element ends a sentence but is not a full sentence of its own, the sentence's period goes outside the closing parenthesis.

n.0: The period belongs to the main sentence, so it goes outside the parenthesis.
n.1: A parenthetical that stands as its own sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with its own period inside the parenthesis.
n.3: No comma goes before an opening parenthesis.

q: A student quotes a nurse who said, "He refused the medication twice." The student wants to show that "He" means Mr. Diaz. Which version of the quotation is punctuated correctly?
o: "He (Mr. Diaz) refused the medication twice."
"He [Mr. Diaz] refused the medication twice."
"He, Mr. Diaz, refused the medication twice."
"He refused the medication twice [sic]."
w: Brackets mark words the writer inserts into someone else's quotation to clarify it.

n.0: Parentheses inside a quotation signal the speaker's own words, not the writer's insertion.
n.2: Commas would present "Mr. Diaz" as part of what the nurse said, changing the quotation.
n.3: [sic] marks an error in the original quotation; this quotation has no error and the name is still not added.

q: A staff newsletter reports on a wellness program. Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
o: Twenty-one nurses joined the self care workshop this year.
Twenty one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the selfcare workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
w: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated, and the prefix self- always takes a hyphen (self-care).

n.0: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, and the compound modifies the noun "workshop".
n.1: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.
n.2: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, not closed up.

q: A hospital recruiting ad describes a surgeon. Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
o: The highly-trained surgeon works a full-time schedule.
The highly trained surgeon works a full-time schedule.
The highly trained surgeon works a full time schedule.
The highly-trained surgeon works a full time schedule.
w: Two rules apply. A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated (a full-time schedule), but no hyphen follows an adverb ending in -ly (highly trained).

n.0: An -ly adverb such as "highly" is not hyphenated to the word it modifies.
n.2: "Full-time" is a compound adjective before the noun "schedule", so it needs a hyphen.
n.3: Both are wrong: "highly trained" takes no hyphen, and "full-time" before a noun needs one.

q: A writing center handout gives six sentences. Which sentences use semicolons and colons correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The tour visits Dayton, Ohio; Erie, Pennsylvania; and Gary, Indiana.
The forms are: the consent, the history, and the release.
The vote was postponed; because the meeting ran late.
Although the meeting ran late; the vote was held.
The kit has one gap: no sterile gloves.
The meeting ran late; therefore, the vote was postponed.
w: A semicolon with a conjunctive adverb joins independent clauses; a colon after a complete clause introduces an explanation; semicolons separate series items that contain commas.

n.1: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "are".
n.2: "Because the meeting ran late" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses.
n.3: "Although the meeting ran late" is a dependent clause, so a comma, not a semicolon, should follow it.

q: A patient is writing about a clinic visit for a hospital blog that follows US conventions. Which sentence punctuates the quotation correctly?
o: The nurse said, "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "Take this with food", and handed me the cup.
The nurse said "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
w: In US style, a comma separates the dialogue tag from the quotation, the quoted sentence begins with a capital letter, and the comma after the quotation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

n.1: A quoted full sentence begins with a capital letter: "Take".
n.2: US style places commas inside the closing quotation mark, not outside.
n.3: A comma is needed after "said" to introduce the quotation.

q: A nursing student is writing about a short poem in a class essay that follows US conventions. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Her favorite poem is "Night Shift at Mercy."
Her favorite poem is Night Shift at Mercy.
Her favorite poem is 'Night Shift at Mercy.'
Her favorite poem is "Night Shift at Mercy".
w: The title of a short work such as a poem goes in quotation marks, and in US style the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.

n.1: The title of a short work such as a poem must be enclosed in quotation marks.
n.2: US style uses double quotation marks; single marks are for a quotation within a quotation.
n.3: Placing the period outside the closing quotation mark is British style, not US style.

q: A family member is repeating a doctor's instruction and asking a question about it. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Did the doctor really say "no visitors."
Did the doctor really say "no visitors?"
Did the doctor really say "no visitors"?
Did the doctor really say "no visitors".
w: The whole sentence is a question, but the quoted words are not. A question mark that belongs to the whole sentence goes outside the closing quotation mark.

n.0: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark.
n.1: The quoted words "no visitors" are not a question, so the question mark does not belong inside the quotation marks.
n.3: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

q: A unit secretary is writing a note about a lost staff badge. Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?
o: The nurses dont know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurses don't know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurse's don't know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurses don't know who's badge was left in the lounge.
w: "Nurses" is a plain plural (no apostrophe), "don't" is a contraction of "do not" (apostrophe where the o is missing), and "whose" is a possessive pronoun (no apostrophe).

n.0: The contraction of "do not" needs an apostrophe: "don't".
n.2: "Nurses" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe.
n.3: "Who's" means "who is"; the possessive needed here is "whose".

q: A receptionist is recording a phone call. Which sentence uses end punctuation correctly?
o: The patient asked, "Whether the clinic would be open on Monday?"
The patient asked whether the clinic would be open on Monday.
The patient asked whether the clinic would be open on Monday?
The patient asked, whether the clinic would be open on Monday.
w: This is an indirect question: it reports what was asked without quoting the exact words, so it ends with a period and takes no comma or quotation marks.

n.0: These are not the patient's exact words, so quotation marks are wrong.
n.2: An indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.
n.3: No comma separates the verb "asked" from the clause that is its object.

q: A nurse is documenting what a worried parent asked at the bedside. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?".
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked "is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished"?
w: The quoted words are a question, so the question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark, and it also ends the sentence; no second end mark is added.

n.0: The question mark already ends the sentence; adding a period doubles the end punctuation.
n.2: A comma should introduce the quotation, and the quoted sentence should begin with a capital letter.
n.3: The question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark.

q: A board member's comment is quoted in a hospital newsletter. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: She called the plan "a good start;" the board disagreed.
She called the plan, "a good start"; the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start," the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start"; the board disagreed.
w: In US style, semicolons and colons go outside the closing quotation mark (only periods and commas go inside).

n.0: A semicolon goes outside the closing quotation mark.
n.1: The quoted words are part of the sentence's structure (the plan is called something), so no comma should introduce them.
n.2: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

q: A student cites a chapter titled Heart Sounds from a textbook titled Clinical Basics. Following US conventions, how should the two titles be formatted?
o: Chapter in italics; textbook in quotation marks
Both titles in quotation marks
Both titles in italics
Chapter in quotation marks; textbook in italics
w: Titles of short works and parts of works (chapters, articles, poems, songs) go in quotation marks; titles of long works (books, journals, films) are italicized.

n.0: This reverses the rule: the part (chapter) takes quotation marks and the whole book is italicized.
n.1: A book is a long work, so its title is italicized, not placed in quotation marks.
n.2: A chapter is a short part of a work, so its title goes in quotation marks.

q: A student is writing about an instructor who asked the class to label a word. Which sentence is punctuated correctly in US style?
o: The instructor said, "Write 'aseptic' on the first line."
The instructor said, 'Write "aseptic" on the first line.'
The instructor said, "Write 'aseptic' on the first line".
The instructor said, "Write "aseptic" on the first line."
w: In US style, the outer quotation uses double quotation marks, a quotation inside it uses single marks, and the period goes inside the closing marks.

n.1: This reverses US style, which puts double marks outside and single marks inside.
n.2: In US style the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
n.3: A quotation within a quotation takes single marks so the reader can tell where each ends.

q: Read the paragraph. (1) The nurse asked, "Have you eaten today?" (2) The patient said that he wasn't hungry. (3) She wondered why he had skipped breakfast? (4) Later, she wrote "poor appetite" in his chart. Which sentence contains an end-punctuation error?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 3 is an indirect question (she wondered why ...), which is a statement and ends with a period, not a question mark.

n.0: Sentence 1 correctly places the question mark inside the quotation, because the quoted words are a question.
n.1: Sentence 2 is an indirect quotation, correctly ending with a period.
n.3: Sentence 4 is a statement ending with a period after the quoted phrase.

q: An editor is checking apostrophes in a community health newsletter. Which sentences use apostrophes correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The clinic changed it's phone number.
The children's clinic closes at five.
The Garcia's are moving to Denver.
Those coats are their's, not ours.
The Garcias' house is on Elm Street.
We'll review the patients' charts today.
w: Children's (irregular plural + 's), Garcias' (plural family name ending in s + apostrophe), and we'll and patients' (contraction and plural possessive) are all correct.

n.0: The possessive pronoun is "its"; "it's" means "it is" or "it has".
n.2: The family name is a plain plural here (the Garcias are moving), so it takes no apostrophe.
n.3: Possessive pronouns such as "theirs" take no apostrophe.

q: A nurse's comment is split by a dialogue tag in a staff story. Which version is punctuated and capitalized correctly?
o: "I can't stay," Leah said. "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay", Leah said, "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay," Leah said, "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay," Leah said, "Because my shift starts at noon."
w: Two steps: the quotation is one sentence interrupted by the tag, so a comma follows the tag and the second part continues in lowercase. In US style the comma after "stay" goes inside the quotation mark.

n.0: A period after "said" would start a new sentence, which would need a capital; but "because ..." continues the first sentence, so a comma is needed.
n.1: In US style the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
n.3: The second part continues the same sentence, so "because" is not capitalized.

q: A public health department is posting its vaccination schedule. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the Monday after Labor Day.
We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the Monday after labor day.
We hold the flu clinic every Fall, starting the Monday after Labor Day.
We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the monday after Labor Day.
w: Days of the week and holidays are proper nouns (Monday, Labor Day), but seasons are not capitalized unless they are part of a name.

n.1: The name of a holiday is a proper noun, so "Labor Day" is capitalized.
n.2: Seasons such as fall are common nouns and are not capitalized.
n.3: Days of the week are proper nouns, so "Monday" is capitalized.

q: A nursing school newsletter describes a faculty meeting. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: The Doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
The Doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
w: A title is capitalized when it comes directly before a name (Professor Kim) but not when it is used as a general noun (the doctor).

n.0: Both are reversed: the general noun is lowercase, and the title before a name is capitalized.
n.1: A title used directly before a name is capitalized: "Professor Kim".
n.3: "Doctor" is used as a general noun after "the", not as a title before a name, so it is lowercase.

q: A new graduate is writing a cover letter about relocating for a nursing job. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: After moving to the Midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
After moving to the Midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
w: A compass word is capitalized when it names a region (the Midwest) but not when it gives a direction (drove south).

n.1: "The Midwest" names a region of the country, so it is capitalized.
n.2: Both are reversed: the region is capitalized and the direction is lowercase.
n.3: "Drove south" gives a direction, not a region, so it is lowercase.

q: A patient is filling out a family contact form. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: My mom said that Aunt Rosa would call Dad tonight.
My Mom said that Aunt Rosa would call Dad tonight.
My mom said that aunt Rosa would call Dad tonight.
My mom said that Aunt Rosa would call dad tonight.
w: A family word is lowercase after a possessive (my mom), capitalized as a title before a name (Aunt Rosa), and capitalized when used in place of a name (Dad).

n.1: After the possessive "my", "mom" is a common noun and is lowercase.
n.2: "Aunt" is a title before the name Rosa, so it is capitalized.
n.3: "Dad" is used as a name here, with no possessive before it, so it is capitalized.

q: A prenursing student is describing her grades in an application essay. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: She passed Biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her english and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her English and Chemistry grades were lower.
w: A specific numbered course is a proper noun (Biology 101). General school subjects are lowercase (chemistry), except languages, which are always capitalized (English).

n.1: A specific course name with a number is capitalized: "Biology 101".
n.2: Languages are proper nouns, so "English" is capitalized even as a subject.
n.3: "Chemistry" is a general subject here, not a course title, so it is lowercase.

q: A disaster relief report describes a shelter. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: The American Red Cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last Winter.
The American red cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near lake Michigan last winter.
w: Every main word of an organization's name (American Red Cross) and a specific place (Lake Michigan) is capitalized; seasons are lowercase.

n.0: Seasons such as winter are common nouns and are lowercase.
n.1: All main words in the organization's name are capitalized: "Red Cross".
n.3: "Lake" is part of the proper name "Lake Michigan", so it is capitalized.

q: A nurse educator is titling a patient handout and must use standard title case. Which title is capitalized correctly?
o: A guide to caring for patients in the home
A Guide to Caring for Patients in the Home
A Guide To Caring For Patients In The Home
a Guide to Caring for Patients in the Home
w: In title case, capitalize the first and last words and all major words (nouns, verbs, adjectives); lowercase articles and short prepositions in the middle (to, for, in, the).

n.0: This is sentence case; title case capitalizes the major words such as Guide, Caring, Patients and Home.
n.2: Short prepositions (to, for, in) and articles (the) in the middle of a title are lowercase in title case.
n.3: The first word of a title is always capitalized, even when it is an article.

q: A clinic's welcome script quotes a nurse whose sentence is interrupted by a tag. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: "when you arrive," the nurse said, "check in at the front desk."
"When you arrive," the nurse said, "check in at the front desk."
"When you arrive," the nurse said, "Check in at the front desk."
"When you arrive," The nurse said, "check in at the front desk."
w: The quotation is one sentence split by a tag, so it begins with a capital letter (When) and the second part continues in lowercase (check).

n.0: A quoted sentence begins with a capital letter: "When".
n.2: The second part continues the same quoted sentence, so "check" is lowercase.
n.3: The tag continues the sentence after a comma, so "the" is lowercase.

q: A student is writing a history paper about nursing. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: During the Civil War, many irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the civil war, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish Immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
w: Named historical events (the Civil War) and nationalities (Irish) are proper nouns; general nouns such as immigrants are lowercase.

n.0: Nationalities are proper adjectives, so "Irish" is capitalized.
n.1: The name of a specific historical event is capitalized: "Civil War".
n.2: "Immigrants" is a common noun and is lowercase.

q: Read the paragraph. (1) Last summer, Jamal volunteered at Mercy Hospital in Ohio. (2) He worked with a nurse named Carla Diaz. (3) Every Friday, he helped the Hospital's chaplain plan services. (4) In September, he started classes at Lakeview Community College. Which sentence contains a capitalization error?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
w: In sentence 3, "hospital" is a general noun (the hospital's chaplain), not part of a name, so it should be lowercase.

n.0: "Mercy Hospital" is a proper name and "Ohio" is a state; "summer" is correctly lowercase.
n.1: "Carla Diaz" is a name, and "nurse" is correctly lowercase.
n.3: "September" is a month and "Lakeview Community College" is a proper name.

q: An editor is checking capitalization in a hospital newsletter. Which sentences are capitalized correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The President of the club called the meeting to order.
The senator met with Governor Ellis on Tuesday.
My sister speaks Spanish and studies psychology.
She was born in the Spring of 2004 in Texas.
Ask your Doctor about the new vaccine.
We drove east on Main Street to the hospital.
w: A title before a name is capitalized (Governor Ellis) but not a general title (the senator); a direction is lowercase (east); a named street, a language and a day are capitalized; a general subject (psychology) is lowercase.

n.0: A title that is not directly before a name (the president of the club) is lowercase.
n.3: Seasons are common nouns, so "spring" is lowercase.
n.4: "Doctor" after a possessive (your doctor) is a general noun and is lowercase.

q: A reporter is writing about a city official's school visit. Which version of the sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: Last Winter, the mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the Mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the mayor visited Northside high school on Oak avenue.
w: Two rules apply. Proper names of a school and a street are capitalized in full (Northside High School, Oak Avenue), but a season and a title used without a name (the mayor) are lowercase.

n.0: Seasons are common nouns, so "winter" is lowercase.
n.1: "Mayor" is not followed by a name, so it is lowercase.
n.3: "High School" and "Avenue" are parts of proper names, so they are capitalized.

q: A student is classifying sentences from a hospital orientation booklet by structure. Which of the following is a compound sentence?
o: The nurse and the aide checked and recorded the vital signs.
The clinic opened early, but the lab stayed closed until nine.
Because the lab was closed, the samples waited until morning.
When the storm hit, the power failed, and the generator started.
w: A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses and no dependent clause. "The clinic opened early" and "the lab stayed closed until nine" are joined by a comma and "but".

n.0: This is a simple sentence: one independent clause with a compound subject (nurse and aide) and a compound verb (checked and recorded).
n.2: This is complex: "Because the lab was closed" is a dependent clause attached to one independent clause.
n.3: This is compound-complex: two independent clauses plus the dependent clause "When the storm hit".

q: A nursing student is reviewing sentence structure before the TEAS. Which of the following is a complex sentence?
o: Although she studied all week, Rosa felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week and felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week, yet she felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week; she still felt nervous before the exam.
w: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. "Although she studied all week" is dependent (it begins with a subordinating conjunction); "Rosa felt nervous before the exam" is independent.

n.1: One subject with two verbs (studied and felt) is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by a comma and "yet" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make a compound sentence.

q: A pharmacy newsletter describes the work of a pharmacist and her intern. Which of the following is a simple sentence?
o: The pharmacist counted the pills while her intern labeled them.
The pharmacist and her intern counted, sorted, and labeled the pills.
The pharmacist counted the pills, and her intern labeled them.
After the pharmacist counted the pills, the intern labeled them, and they left.
w: A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause. A compound subject (pharmacist and intern) and a series of verbs (counted, sorted, and labeled) still form one clause.

n.0: "While her intern labeled them" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by ", and" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses plus the dependent clause "After the pharmacist counted the pills" make it compound-complex.

q: Read the sentence from a shift report: "When the shift ended, Maya charted her notes, and Luis restocked the supply cart." Which statement correctly describes the structure of this sentence?
o: It is compound-complex because it has two independent clauses and a dependent clause.
It is complex because it opens with the dependent clause "When the shift ended."
It is compound because two independent clauses are joined by a comma and "and."
It is simple because it has one subject performing a series of related actions.
w: The sentence has two independent clauses (Maya charted her notes; Luis restocked the supply cart) and one dependent clause (When the shift ended), so it is compound-complex.

n.1: A complex sentence has only one independent clause; this one has two.
n.2: A compound sentence has no dependent clause; this one also has "When the shift ended".
n.3: There are two subjects (Maya, Luis) with their own verbs, so there are two independent clauses, not one.

q: An infection-control poster uses sentences with different purposes. Which sentence is imperative?
o: You washed your hands before you entered the patient's room.
Did you wash your hands before you entered the patient's room?
Please wash your hands before you enter the patient's room.
What a relief it was to wash my hands after that long shift!
w: An imperative sentence gives a command or makes a request, with the subject "you" understood: "[You] Please wash your hands."

n.0: This makes a statement, so it is declarative.
n.1: This asks a question, so it is interrogative.
n.3: This expresses strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

q: Read the sentence: "The patient's fever broke overnight; therefore, the doctor canceled the blood culture." How is this sentence classified by structure?
o: Compound
Simple
Complex
Compound-complex
w: Both parts are independent clauses. "Therefore" is a conjunctive adverb, not a subordinating conjunction, so it does not create a dependent clause; a semicolon joins the two clauses, making the sentence compound.

n.1: There are two independent clauses, not one.
n.2: "Therefore" does not make the second clause dependent, so there is no dependent clause.
n.3: Compound-complex needs a dependent clause, and this sentence has none.

q: A nursing instructor asks students to identify a compound-complex sentence in a set of examples. Which sentence is compound-complex?
o: Ana and Ben missed the bus and arrived late to the lecture.
Because Ana missed the bus, she arrived late to the lecture.
Ana arrived on time, but Ben, who missed the bus, was late.
Ana missed the bus, so she arrived late to the lecture.
w: Two independent clauses (Ana arrived on time; Ben was late) plus a dependent relative clause (who missed the bus) make a compound-complex sentence.

n.0: One independent clause with a compound subject and compound verb is a simple sentence.
n.1: One dependent clause and one independent clause make a complex sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.

q: Read the two sentences: "The clinic ran out of flu vaccine. Staff placed a new order." Which option combines them into a complex sentence?
o: The clinic ran out of flu vaccine; staff placed a new order.
When the clinic ran out of flu vaccine, staff placed a new order.
The clinic ran out of flu vaccine, so staff placed a new order.
The clinic ran out of flu vaccine and then placed a new order.
w: Adding the subordinating conjunction "When" turns the first clause into a dependent clause, so the result has one dependent and one independent clause: a complex sentence.

n.0: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, making a compound sentence.
n.2: A comma and "so" join two independent clauses, making a compound sentence.
n.3: This has one subject with two verbs, so it is a simple sentence (and it changes who placed the order).

q: A student is checking whether sentences about a retired nurse contain a dependent clause. Which sentence is complex?
o: The nurse trained me, and she retired last spring.
The nurse who trained me retired last spring.
The nurse trained me and retired last spring.
Trained by experts, the nurse retired last spring.
w: Two steps: "who trained me" has its own subject (who) and verb (trained), so it is a dependent relative clause; with the independent clause "The nurse retired last spring", the sentence is complex.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.
n.2: One subject with two verbs is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.3: "Trained by experts" is a participial phrase (no subject-verb pair), so the sentence is simple.

q: Read the paragraph. (1) Kayla works nights at a nursing home. (2) She checks on residents and updates their charts. (3) When a resident cannot sleep, she brings warm milk. (4) Her job is tiring, but she loves it. Which sentence is complex?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 3 has a dependent clause (When a resident cannot sleep) and an independent clause (she brings warm milk), so it is complex.

n.0: Sentence 1 is simple: one independent clause.
n.1: Sentence 2 is simple: one subject with a compound verb (checks and updates).
n.3: Sentence 4 is compound: two independent clauses joined by ", but".

q: A tutor gives a student six sentences from a patient handout. Which sentences are simple sentences? Select all that apply.
o: The staff stayed calm because the night was quiet.
If the form is signed, the nurse will file it.
The aide lifted the patient, and the nurse adjusted the bed.
The aide lifted the patient carefully and adjusted the bed.
Both the doctor and the nurse signed the form.
During the long night shift, the staff stayed calm.
w: Each simple sentence has one independent clause: a compound subject, an introductory prepositional phrase or a compound verb does not add a clause.

n.0: "Because the night was quiet" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.1: "If the form is signed" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by ", and" make a compound sentence.

q: A writer wants to turn "The doctor reviewed the X-ray, and she ordered a CT scan" into a simple sentence without changing its meaning. Which revision does this correctly?
o: After the doctor reviewed the X-ray, she ordered a CT scan.
The doctor, who reviewed the X-ray, ordered a CT scan.
The doctor reviewed the X-ray; she ordered a CT scan.
The doctor reviewed the X-ray and ordered a CT scan.
w: Removing the second subject (she) leaves one subject with a compound predicate (reviewed ... and ordered): one independent clause, a simple sentence.

n.0: "After the doctor reviewed the X-ray" is a dependent clause, so the result is complex.
n.1: "Who reviewed the X-ray" is a dependent relative clause, so the result is complex.
n.2: A semicolon joining two independent clauses still makes a compound sentence.

q: A student is labeling word groups taken from a patient education leaflet. Which group of words is a dependent clause?
o: during the long night shift
the nurse finished her charting
running down the hospital hallway
because the pharmacy was closed
w: A dependent clause has a subject and a verb (the pharmacy was) but begins with a subordinating conjunction (because), so it cannot stand alone.

n.0: This is a prepositional phrase: it has no subject-verb pair.
n.1: This has a subject and verb and expresses a complete thought, so it is an independent clause.
n.2: This is a participial phrase: "running" is a verbal with no subject.

q: Read the sentence: "After the meeting, the staff ate lunch in the break room." What is the word group "After the meeting"?
o: An appositive phrase
An independent clause
A prepositional phrase
A dependent clause
w: "After" works here as a preposition with the object "the meeting". There is no verb, so the group is a phrase, not a clause.

n.0: An appositive renames a nearby noun; "After the meeting" tells when, it does not rename anything.
n.1: An independent clause needs a subject and verb and must express a complete thought.
n.3: A dependent clause needs a subject and a verb (for example, "After the meeting ended"); this group has no verb.

q: A clinic's front-desk assistant is writing a schedule note. Which sentence uses the articles "a" and "an" correctly?
o: The aide waited an hour before ordering a uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering a uniform.
w: The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter: "an hour" (silent h, vowel sound) and "a uniform" (begins with a "you" consonant sound).

n.1: Both are reversed: "an hour" and "a uniform".
n.2: "Uniform" begins with a consonant "y" sound, so it takes "a".
n.3: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes "an".

q: Read the sentence: "The nurse carefully explained the very complex procedure." Which word is an adverb that modifies an adjective?
o: complex
explained
very
carefully
w: "Very" is an adverb that modifies the adjective "complex", telling how complex the procedure is.

n.0: "Complex" is the adjective being modified; it describes the noun "procedure".
n.1: "Explained" is the verb of the sentence.
n.3: "Carefully" is an adverb, but it modifies the verb "explained", not an adjective.

q: Read the sentence: "Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff report to the lobby." Which part of the sentence is the independent clause?
o: Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff
the staff report to the lobby
Whenever the alarm sounds
to the lobby
w: "The staff report to the lobby" has a subject (staff) and a verb (report) and can stand alone as a sentence.

n.0: This joins the dependent clause to the subject but leaves out the verb, so it is not a clause.
n.2: "Whenever" is a subordinating conjunction, so this clause is dependent.
n.3: "To the lobby" is a prepositional phrase with no subject or verb.

q: Read the sentence: "Walking every day lowers blood pressure." How does the phrase "Walking every day" function?
o: As an infinitive phrase acting as an adverb
As the main verb of the sentence
As a gerund phrase acting as a noun
As a participial phrase acting as an adjective
w: "Walking every day" is the subject of the verb "lowers". An -ing verbal used as a noun is a gerund, so this is a gerund phrase acting as a noun.

n.0: An infinitive phrase begins with "to" (to walk).
n.1: The main verb is "lowers"; an -ing word without a helping verb cannot be the main verb.
n.3: A participial phrase modifies a noun; this phrase is itself the subject.

q: Read the sentence: "Smiling at the child, the nurse gave the injection." What is "Smiling at the child"?
o: A participial phrase modifying "nurse"
A gerund phrase acting as the subject
A dependent clause modifying "gave"
An infinitive phrase showing purpose
w: "Smiling at the child" is an -ing verbal phrase that describes the nurse, so it is a participial phrase acting as an adjective.

n.1: The subject of the sentence is "the nurse"; the phrase describes the subject rather than acting as it.
n.2: A clause needs a subject and a verb; this phrase has no subject.
n.3: An infinitive phrase begins with "to".

q: A student is studying verbal phrases for an English quiz. Which sentence contains an infinitive phrase?
o: The patient went to the cafeteria after lunch.
The patient wanted to rest after lunch.
The patient resting after lunch felt better.
Resting after lunch helped the patient.
w: An infinitive is "to" + the base form of a verb: "to rest" (to rest after lunch) is an infinitive phrase.

n.0: "To the cafeteria" is "to" + a noun, which is a prepositional phrase, not an infinitive.
n.2: "Resting after lunch" is a participial phrase describing "patient".
n.3: "Resting after lunch" is a gerund phrase acting as the subject.

q: A staff memo describes a charge nurse in several ways. Which sentence contains an appositive phrase?
o: Ms. Lee, the charge nurse, approved the schedule.
Ms. Lee, approving the schedule, thanked the charge nurse.
Ms. Lee approved the schedule for the charge nurse.
Ms. Lee, who is the charge nurse, approved the schedule.
w: An appositive phrase is a noun phrase that renames the noun beside it: "the charge nurse" renames Ms. Lee.

n.1: "Approving the schedule" is a participial phrase.
n.2: "For the charge nurse" is a prepositional phrase.
n.3: "Who is the charge nurse" has a subject and a verb, so it is a relative (dependent) clause, not a phrase.

q: Read the sentence: "The aide remained on the unit because it was busy, so she skipped lunch until three." Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
o: remained
until
so
because
w: "Because" introduces the dependent clause "because it was busy", so it is a subordinating conjunction.

n.0: "Remained" is the main verb of the independent clause, not a conjunction.
n.1: "Until" is followed only by "three" (no subject or verb), so here it is a preposition.
n.2: "So" joins two independent clauses here, so it is a coordinating conjunction.

q: Read the sentence: "The patient seemed anxious before surgery." What part of speech is "anxious" in this sentence?
o: Adjective modifying "patient"
Noun acting as a subject complement
Adverb modifying "seemed"
Verb completing "seemed"
w: "Seemed" is a linking verb, so the word after it describes the subject: "anxious" is a predicate adjective describing "patient".

n.1: "Anxious" describes the patient rather than naming something; a noun complement would rename the subject (for example, "seemed a calm patient").
n.2: After a linking verb the describing word modifies the subject (a noun), so it is an adjective; the adverb form would be "anxiously".
n.3: The whole verb is "seemed"; "anxious" is not a verb form, so it cannot complete the verb.

q: Read the sentence: "The nurse who works nights trained the student whom we hired." How many dependent clauses does it contain?
o: Three
Zero
Two
One
w: There are two relative clauses, each with its own subject and verb: "who works nights" and "whom we hired". The independent clause is "The nurse trained the student".

n.0: "The nurse trained the student" is the independent clause, so it is not counted.
n.1: Clauses beginning with relative pronouns (who, whom) are dependent clauses.
n.3: Both "who works nights" and "whom we hired" are dependent clauses, not just one.

q: A charge nurse is reviewing statements in a staff training packet. Which of the following is a complete sentence?
o: The nurse who works nights trained the new aide.
Because the nurse who works nights trained the aide.
Running to the clinic before the nurse's night shift.
The nurse who works nights and trains the new aides.
w: "The nurse ... trained the new aide" has a subject (nurse), a main verb (trained) and a complete thought; "who works nights" is a relative clause inside it.

n.1: "Because" makes the whole word group a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.2: This is a participial phrase with no subject and no main verb.
n.3: The verbs "works" and "trains" both belong to the relative clause beginning with "who", so "The nurse" has no main verb: a fragment.

q: An editor is checking a clinic newsletter for sentence errors. Which of the following is a comma splice?
o: The bus was late; we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, so we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, we missed the appointment.
Because the bus was late, we missed the appointment.
w: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. "The bus was late" and "we missed the appointment" can each stand alone.

n.0: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
n.1: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction "so" correctly joins two independent clauses.
n.3: The first clause is dependent (Because ...), so a comma after it is correct.

q: Read the run-on sentence from an incident report: "The power went out the generator started within seconds." Which revision corrects it?
o: The power went out, however the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, the generator started within seconds.
The power went out and, the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, and the generator started within seconds.
w: A comma followed by a coordinating conjunction (and) correctly joins two independent clauses.

n.0: "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma before it still leaves a comma splice.
n.1: Adding only a comma turns the run-on into a comma splice.
n.2: The comma must come before the conjunction, not after it.

q: Read the paragraph from a clinic flyer. (1) The clinic offers free flu shots. (2) Every Saturday from nine to noon. (3) Patients should bring their insurance cards. (4) Walk-ins are welcome. Which sentence is a fragment?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 2 has no subject and no verb; it is a group of prepositional phrases telling when. It could be joined to sentence 1.

n.0: Sentence 1 has a subject (clinic) and a verb (offers) and is complete.
n.2: Sentence 3 has a subject (Patients) and a verb (should bring) and is complete.
n.3: Sentence 4 has a subject (Walk-ins) and a verb (are) and is complete.

q: Read the sentence from a nursing note: "The patient felt dizzy, however, she refused to sit down." Which revision corrects the comma splice?
o: The patient felt dizzy, she, however, refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy, however she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy; however, she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy however, she refused to sit down.
w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

n.0: Moving "however" inside the second clause still leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma.
n.1: A comma before "however" still joins two independent clauses with only a comma: a comma splice.
n.3: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.

q: Read the word groups from a medication note: "Because the patient was allergic to penicillin. The doctor prescribed a different antibiotic." Which revision correctly fixes the fragment?
o: Because the patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin; the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin the doctor, prescribed a different antibiotic.
The patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
w: The dependent clause (Because ... penicillin) is attached to the independent clause with a comma, giving a correct complex sentence.

n.1: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the first part is a dependent clause.
n.2: The comma is misplaced: it separates the subject (the doctor) from its verb, and the comma after the introductory clause is missing.
n.3: Removing "Because" leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma: a comma splice.

q: A unit manager is editing a weekly staffing update. Which of the following sentences is structured correctly?
o: The clinic was short-staffed on Friday. Because several walk-ins arrived before nine.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
Although the clinic was short-staffed, the nurses kept every visit on schedule.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday, several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
w: A dependent clause (Although the clinic was short-staffed) followed by a comma and an independent clause is a correct complex sentence.

n.0: The second word group begins with "Because" and has no independent clause, so it is a fragment.
n.1: Two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.

q: A student is checking notes from a clinical rotation. Which of the following is a fragment?
o: Hoping to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
She hoped to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
Finish your charting before the end of the shift.
Hoping to finish, she charted before the end of the shift.
w: Two steps: "Hoping" is a participle, not a main verb, and the word group has no subject, so it cannot stand alone.

n.1: This has a subject (She) and a main verb (hoped), so it is complete.
n.2: This is an imperative sentence; its subject "you" is understood, so it is complete.
n.3: The participial phrase is attached to the independent clause "she charted ...", so it is complete.

q: Read the paragraph from a hand-hygiene poster. (1) Hand hygiene prevents infection. (2) Staff should wash for at least twenty seconds they should also dry their hands fully. (3) Sanitizer works when hands are not visibly soiled. (4) Gloves do not replace washing. Which sentence is a run-on?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 2 runs two independent clauses (Staff should wash ...; they should also dry ...) together with no punctuation or conjunction.

n.0: Sentence 1 is a single independent clause.
n.2: Sentence 3 is a complex sentence: an independent clause plus the dependent clause "when hands are not visibly soiled".
n.3: Sentence 4 is a single independent clause.

q: Read the comma splice: "The roads were icy, the clinic opened late." Which revision corrects the error and shows that the icy roads caused the late opening?
o: Although the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
Because the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
The roads were icy, the clinic, therefore, opened late.
The roads were icy, but the clinic opened late.
w: Two steps: subordinating one clause fixes the splice, and "Because" signals cause and effect.

n.0: "Although" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.
n.2: The two independent clauses are still joined by only a comma, so the splice remains.
n.3: "But" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.

q: A nurse is writing patient instructions and wants every line to be a complete sentence. Which of the following is a complete sentence?
o: Please sign the consent form before the procedure.
The consent form that was signed before the procedure.
Since the consent form was signed before the procedure.
Signing the consent form before the procedure.
w: An imperative sentence is complete even though its subject (you) is not stated: "[You] Please sign the consent form."

n.1: "That was signed ..." is a relative clause describing the form; the subject "The consent form" has no main verb.
n.2: "Since" makes this a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.3: This is a gerund phrase with no main verb.

q: Read the sentence: "The reason the test was delayed is because the machine broke." Which revision corrects the faulty sentence structure?
o: The reason the test was delayed, is that the machine broke.
The reason the test was delayed is because of the machine broke.
The reason the test was delayed is that the machine broke.
The reason the test was delayed is when the machine broke.
w: "The reason ... is" must be completed by a noun clause (that the machine broke), not an adverb clause beginning with "because". This repairs the faulty predication.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject (The reason the test was delayed) from its verb (is).
n.1: "Because of" must be followed by a noun phrase, not a clause with a verb (broke).
n.3: "Is when" is also faulty predication: a reason is not a time.
